Random-policy rollout • CartPole
loop
An agent sees four measurements and chooses left or right. A reward of one counts another surviving step. A rollout collects experience; it does not yet learn.
Inspect reset and the five step outputs. Seed resets and the action generator independently. End the episode on termination OR truncation. Run headless before enabling human rendering.
Compare 30 random episodes across seeds 0–4. Record lengths and why each episode ended. Change max-steps from 500 to 50; explain why this changes the measured return.
Precursor: random search and feedback control. Compare a hand-coded pole-angle controller, then cross-entropy search as an optional algorithm.
Environment → observation → policy → action → transition logger. Separate rendering from collection; log seed, environment version, cap and end reason.
At a time limit, must collection stop?
Yes. Stop collection on truncation, but a value target can still bootstrap if the underlying task continues.
First-visit Monte Carlo control • Blackjack
mc
Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + [G − Q(s,a)] / N(s,a)
Play a whole hand before assigning credit. Average returns from the first occurrence of each state/action in a hand. Epsilon exploration prevents an early lucky hand from freezing the policy.
Trace one trajectory forward, returns backward, and first visits forward. Use the full tuple (player sum, dealer card, usable ace), not just the player sum.
Train 50,000 hands between sessions; compare epsilon .05/.1/.2 over five seeds. Evaluate the frozen greedy table on separate seeds. Report mean return and win/draw/loss frequencies.
Precursor: sample-average estimation. Alternative: every-visit MC and Q-learning on the same Blackjack environment; implement the latter as the optional comparison, reusing session 3.
Online episodic collector → trajectory buffer → return computation → table and visit-count checkpoint. Blackjack needs no learned world model.
Does first-visit mean the first visit across all training?
No. It means the first occurrence of that state/action pair within each episode.
Masked Q-learning • Taxi-v4
q
Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a)+α[r+γ max_valid Q(s′,·)−Q(s,a)]
Learn what the best next action could achieve even while exploring. The mask excludes no-effect actions and illegal pickup/drop-off choices under the environment convention.

Adapt your taxi/action_masking_taxi.py. Mask random actions, greedy actions, and next-state maxima. Always update the last transition; terminal target is the reward. Do not silently treat truncation as terminal.

Paired seeds 0–4, 5,000 episodes, masked versus unmasked, same budgets. Report both exploration returns and separate greedy evaluation. Count invalid actions; do not claim every mask guarantees safety outside this task.
Precursor: TD(0). Alternatives: SARSA, Expected SARSA, double Q-learning. Optional environment transfer: run --env Blackjack-v1 and compare with MC.
Mask belongs to the observation contract. Use the mask from the NEXT observation for the target. Audit action availability drift between training and deployment.
If terminal reward is +20 and all Q values are zero, what target is used?
20. Skipping the terminal update prevents the pickup/drop-off reward from propagating correctly.
SARSA • CliffWalking and FrozenLake
sarsa
Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a)+α[r+γ Q(s′,a′)−Q(s,a)]
SARSA learns the consequence of the action its exploratory policy actually takes next. Near a cliff, this can favor a wider route because exploration remains risky.
Carry the sampled next action into the next iteration. Compare --algo sarsa and --algo q on CliffWalking-v1. Transfer to FrozenLake-v1 with slippery transitions.
Cliff: compare training return versus greedy route. FrozenLake: run at least 10,000 episodes and evaluate success probability, not just a single lucky trajectory. Keep map and slipperiness fixed.
Precursor: TD prediction. Alternatives: off-policy Q-learning, Expected SARSA and n-step SARSA. Optional planning lab: value iteration with the known FrozenLake transition model.
Online behavior policy and target policy coincide for SARSA. Save the exploration schedule; a deployed greedy policy differs from the training policy.
Why can SARSA take a safer route than Q-learning during exploration?
Its target includes the actual exploratory next action, so exploratory falls influence the learned value.
Semi-gradient Q-learning • linear approximation
linear
w ← w + α [r+γ max_a q(s′,a;w)−q(s,a;w)] ∇w q(s,a;w)
A continuous CartPole observation cannot have one row per possible state. Shared weights generalize across nearby states, but bad updates now affect many predictions.
Use a linear map from four observations to two action values. Detach the bootstrap target. Compare feature scales and learning rates; inspect exploding values.
Run lr .0003/.001/.01 over five seeds. Record TD loss and episode return. Add normalized features as a homework ablation. A short run is a plumbing check, not convergence evidence.
Precursor: tabular TD. Alternatives: tile coding, radial-basis features, fitted Q iteration. The deadly triad combines approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning.
Feature pipeline → shared estimator → semi-gradient update. Freeze feature statistics for evaluation. Record feature transforms with weights.
Why detach the TD target?
Semi-gradient learning treats the target as fixed for that update rather than differentiating through its bootstrap estimate.
DQN • replay and target networks
dqn
y = r + γ(1−terminated) max_a Q_target(s′,a)
Replay revisits old experience; a delayed target network slows the moving target. These stabilize a neural Q learner but do not guarantee success.
Inspect replay tuples, sampled batches and target sync every 100 optimizer updates. Confirm no gradient reaches the target network. Use CartPole before image observations.
Between sessions train 300–1,000 episodes, five seeds. Ablate replay or target lag one at a time. Report environment steps, return, wall time and evaluation policy.
Precursors: neural fitted Q iteration, experience replay. Alternatives: Double DQN, dueling networks, distributional RL; none is silently included in this minimal DQN.
Actor → replay storage → learner → target synchronizer → checkpoint → evaluator. Store termination separately from time limits. Larger replay can introduce stale behavior.
Is DQN on-policy because it collects fresh experience?
No. Its greedy target differs from the exploratory behavior, and replay uses older transitions.
REINFORCE • policy gradients
reinforce
∇J ≈ Σ_t G_t ∇ log πθ(A_t|S_t)
Increase the probability of actions that occurred before good returns. Stochastic action sampling supplies exploration without an epsilon-greedy Q table.
Build a categorical policy; retain differentiable log probabilities when recomputing a trajectory. Use full Monte Carlo returns. Inspect the negative sign required by a minimizing optimizer.
Compare raw returns with a running scalar baseline as an exercise. Run 300 episodes and five seeds; plot gradient norms and return variability.
Precursor: score-function estimator. Alternatives: reward-to-go, learned baselines, natural gradients and actor-critic. Discount conventions must match the declared objective.
Policy sampler → complete episode → return estimator → optimizer. The supplied version uses reward-to-go as a common practical surrogate; finite rollout cutoffs bias continuing-task returns.
Can a baseline depend on the sampled action without correction?
Generally no. An action-independent baseline preserves the expected policy gradient; arbitrary action dependence can bias it.
PPO-Clip • actor-critic bridge
ppo
L = E[min(r_t A_t, clip(r_t,1−ε,1+ε) A_t)]
An actor chooses actions and a critic estimates their prospects. PPO reuses a rollout for several updates while clipping the probability ratio objective. Clipping is not a hard KL constraint.
Read the supplied compact episodic actor-critic and PPO branches. Snapshot old log probabilities, detach advantages, train the critic, and recompute current probabilities each epoch.

In class run two short episodes and inspect ratios. Between sessions compare 1 versus 4 update epochs and seeds 0–4. Add approximate KL logging, advantage normalization and GAE in an optional session.
Precursor: actor-critic and TRPO. Alternatives: A2C and PPO with KL penalty. Optional session 8A dedicates 90 minutes to actor-critic before PPO.
Rollout actor → old-policy logprobs → returns/advantages → clipped actor and value losses → policy version. This educational implementation uses one episode per batch, no GAE or vectorization.
Does clipping guarantee a fixed KL divergence?
No. Monitor empirical KL; the clipped surrogate alone does not enforce a hard trust region.
Supervised fine-tuning • pretraining → RLHF
sft
§3.1 and §13.1 are conceptual bridges, not sources for SFT; InstructGPT §3
L_SFT = −Σ log πθ(y_t | prompt,y_<t)
Pretraining learns next-token prediction on broad text. SFT uses demonstrations of desired responses. RLHF adds preference labels, a reward model and a policy optimization stage; SFT alone is not RL.
Train the bundled four-prompt, three-token conditional model. Identify prompt IDs, target tokens and cross entropy. Trace how completion-only masking extends this one-token objective to sequences.
Compare demonstration noise levels in an exercise and record held-out prompt accuracy after designing a feature-sharing model. The supplied lookup model cannot generalize to unseen prompt IDs.
Precursor: maximum likelihood and imitation learning. Alternatives: behavioral cloning, rejection sampling fine-tuning. Optional 9A: tiny autoregressive transformer and response-token loss masks.
Corpus → tokenizer → pretraining → demonstrations/SFT → preference collection → reward model → PPO/RLHF → evaluation. Keep annotator consent, data provenance and split boundaries explicit.
Is a preference pair equivalent to a demonstration?
No. A pair orders two responses; a demonstration specifies the response whose likelihood SFT should increase.
Direct Preference Optimization
dpo
§13.1 conceptual bridge; DPO paper §§3–4 (not in Sutton & Barto)
L_DPO = −log σ(β[(logπw−logπref,w)−(logπl−logπref,l)])
Given a preferred and rejected response, increase their policy-versus-reference log-ratio gap. Standard DPO uses a fixed offline pair dataset and needs no rollout sampling during its update.

Inspect chosen/rejected token indices and freeze reference log probabilities. Verify zero relative margin yields log(2). Sequence extensions sum response-token log probabilities under identical tokenization.
Sweep beta .05/.1/.5, flip 20% of preference labels, and compare preference accuracy and reference KL. Toy correctness is objective verification, not evidence of human preference alignment.

Precursors: Bradley–Terry preference likelihood and KL-regularized RL. Alternatives: reward modeling plus PPO, IPO, online preference collection. DPO can be placed inside an online data-refresh system.
Versioned prompts/pairs → fixed reference scorer → policy trainer → held-out preference evaluator. Audit pair leakage, response length and reference/tokenizer consistency.
Does standard DPO need a separately trained reward model?
No. Its objective uses preference pairs and a fixed reference policy, with an implicit reward interpretation.
Group Relative Policy Optimization
grpo
§13.4 conceptual baseline bridge; DeepSeekMath §4
A_i = (r_i−mean_group r)/(std_group r+ε)
Sample several answers for the same prompt and compare each reward with its group. A learned critic is replaced by group-relative advantages; the reward signal can still be wrong.
Generate eight one-token completions per prompt. Detach group advantages and old log probabilities. Inspect the clipped surrogate and positive sampled KL estimator relative to the fixed reference.
Vary group size 2/8/16 as an exercise; measure zero-variance groups, reward and exact categorical KL. Compare rollout cost. Uniformly correct or incorrect groups have zero relative advantage.

Precursor: REINFORCE with baselines and PPO. Alternatives: PPO with critic, leave-one-out baselines and later GRPO variants. The included one-token formulation is not a reproduction of DeepSeekMath training.
Prompt sampler → grouped policy rollouts → deterministic verifier → group normalization → old-policy ratios/reference KL → optimizer. Fresh samples make the loop online.
What signal comes from a group with identical rewards?
The normalized reward advantages are zero; the KL term may still update the policy.
Monte Carlo policy evaluation • capstone harness
evaluate
V̂π = (1/N) Σ_i G_i; SE ≈ s/√N
Freeze a policy and estimate how well it performs on fresh episodes. Evaluation is an algorithm with a sampling distribution, not a screenshot of one successful run.
Load a saved Q table with --resume and use --algo evaluate. It selects greedy actions without updating values. Use the multi-seed harness for training runs, then separate evaluation seeds.

Capstone: Taxi masked/unmasked or Cliff SARSA/Q comparison; or DPO/GRPO toy objective audit. Submit raw metrics, protocol, confidence intervals, architecture and failure analysis. Do not compare toy rewards to published LLM benchmarks.

Precursor: sample means. Alternatives: bootstrap intervals and paired differences; offline importance sampling requires behavior propensities and support. Logged online returns are not off-policy evaluation.
Immutable checkpoint → isolated evaluator → seed/prompt split → metric aggregation → report. Distinguish online interaction, offline replay learning and fixed offline datasets.
Can many episodes from one training seed establish training robustness?
No. They estimate that policy’s evaluation variability; use independently trained seeds to measure training variability.
